Step 0 · Average velocity is not enough

Average velocity is not enough: it answers for an interval, not for an instant

A car moves along a line with displacement s = t² (after t seconds it has gone t² metres). Average velocity is easy: displacement over a stretch divided by the time that stretch took. But the coach asks something else — “at the instant t = 1 s, exactly how fast is it?” Drag the time probe to see where it is at each moment, then try the three intervals: the right end pulls in from 3 s to 1.5 s — watch what the average velocity does.

Play ▶
Not started: t = 1 s (small step 10 / 30)
Time probe t (seconds) t = 1 s

Time probe: at t = 1 s the displacement is s = t² = 1 m. That is “where it is at each moment” — not yet “how fast at this moment”.

Pick an interval and compute its average velocity:
[1, 3]
[1, 2]
[1, 1.5]

On [1, 3]: s(1) = 1 m, s(3) = 9 m, Δs = 8 m, Δt = 2 s, average velocity = Δs ÷ Δt = 4 m/s. That is an average over a full two seconds — it answers “how fast on average over this stretch”, not the instant t = 1. Narrow the interval and try again.

Two terms to fix in place: displacement over a stretch of time is called the average rate of change over that stretch (here: the average velocity); the rate “at one instant” is the instantaneous rate of change. The average depends on the interval and cannot answer for an instant; to ask about an instant, the interval must shrink to a point — the next step does exactly that, in geometric clothes.

The Play button walks the probe from t = 0 to t = 3 along the curve: the later it gets, the farther it travels in the same 0.1 s — the speed itself is changing, which is exactly why an “average” cannot answer for “this instant”.
